passages.happening:
God says Ezekiel lives among a rebellious house who ‘have eyes to see but do not see, and ears to hear but do not hear’ (verse 2). So he is to pack his bags for exile in broad daylight while they watch, dig through the wall in the evening, and carry his belongings out at dusk on his shoulder, with his face covered so that he cannot see the land (verses 3-6). Ezekiel does it (verse 7).

In the morning God explains. ‘This burden concerns the prince in Jerusalem’ (verse 10). Like Ezekiel, the prince will go out at dusk through a hole in the wall with his face covered. God will catch him in his net and bring him to Babylon, ‘yet he will not see it, and there he will die’ (verse 13). His troops will be scattered, and a few will survive to tell the nations what Israel had done (verses 14-16).
passages.hearers:
An exile's bag was small. Deportees carried only what they could lift, and Assyrian reliefs show lines of captives walking with sacks over their shoulders. The watching exiles had made the same trip a few years before. Houses in Mesopotamia were built of mud brick, so digging through a wall by hand was possible, and it pictured escape through a breach in a city wall.

The prince is Zedekiah, Judah's last king, whom Ezekiel calls prince rather than king. When the wall was breached he fled by night, was caught near Jericho, saw his sons killed, was blinded, and was taken to Babylon in chains. That history explains the riddle: he would come to Babylon and not see it.
passages.later: When the city was breached, ‘all the men of war fled by night’ (2 Kings 25:4). The king was blinded and taken to Babylon, where he was kept ‘until his dying day’ (Jeremiah 52:11).
passages.asks: The people watched Ezekiel act out exile and still did not understand. Ask what warnings you have watched without taking in. And ask what it would take for you to see.

passages.happening:
God tells Ezekiel to eat his bread with trembling and drink his water with anxiety, a sign that the people of Jerusalem will eat and drink in dread because the land will be stripped for its violence (verses 17-20).

The people had a proverb: ‘The days go by, and every vision fails’ (verse 22). God will end it. ‘The days are at hand when every vision will be fulfilled’ (verse 23). Others said Ezekiel's visions were about the distant future (verse 27). God answers, ‘None of My words will be delayed any longer’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
The proverb shows how prophecy could be brushed aside in daily talk. Prophets had warned of judgment for generations, and every year the city did not fall made the warnings sound emptier. The second saying was gentler but just as dismissive: perhaps it will happen, but not in this generation.

God's answer is that the delay was patience, not failure, and it is over. Flattering visions, the false prophets' promises of peace, will end as well.
passages.later: Habakkuk was told, ‘Though it lingers, wait for it, since it will surely come and will not delay’ (Habakkuk 2:3). Isaiah heard scoffers say of God, ‘Let Him hurry and hasten His work’ (Isaiah 5:19).
passages.asks: The people thought God's warnings were always for someday. Ask what you are putting off because it seems far away. And ask what it would mean to act as if God's word matters today.
